Every checkpoint is first scored on at most 400 utterances from the deterministic one-in-50 LibriSpeech-100 chain holdout. Direct validation computes COMET for stable partial-audio targets and complete-audio translations, and ranks checkpoints by their equal-weight mean. The top two candidates undergo autoregressive FLEURS-development rollouts over τ ∈ { − 0.8 , − 0.6 , − 0.3 , 0.0 , 0.3 , 0.6 , 0.8 , 0.9 , 1.0 } \tau\in\{-0.8,-0.6,-0.3,0.0,0.3,0.6,0.8,0.9,1.0\} . A full-audio quality gate requires the candidate’s τ = 1.0 \tau{=}1.0 COMET to remain within 0.5 0.5 of the base self-teacher. Among eligible candidates, mean attainable COMET over a shared latency-budget grid determines the selection; the direct score breaks ties. Multi-turn append-only decoding. Controlled validation on the same deterministic holdout evaluates productive partial contexts and final contexts with gold causal history. The productive-partial COMET champion and WAIT-balanced-accuracy champion form the shortlist. These candidates then undergo append-only autoregressive development rollouts over the same nine confidence thresholds, and mean attainable COMET over their shared latency support determines the selected checkpoint. 3.7 Inference Mechanisms and Metrics All inference mechanisms receive the same sequence of audio blocks and preserve the previously committed target. The confidence mechanism compares the highest non-EOS continuation probability with the EOS probability and emits only when their margin exceeds threshold τ \tau ; sweeping τ \tau traces a model’s quality–latency frontier. We compare it with wait- k k and target-suffix deletion ( Ma et al., 2019 ; Arivazhagan et al., 2020 ) . Wait- k k suppresses writing for a fixed number of initial 2 2 s blocks, while suffix deletion withholds a fixed number of trailing target units from each non-final delta. Translation quality is measured with COMET-22-DA ( Rei et al., 2022 ) . Latency is measured with Average Lagging in seconds, using audio blocks rather than source-token position, as defined in Appendix A , Equation 5 . We evaluate the selected single-turn forced-prefix decoding and multi-turn append-only decoding models on FLEURS primarily, and on CoVoST 2 at the end. We report each complete frontier rather than a single operating point, and include the complete-audio translation as the offline endpoint. Commit calibration is evaluated on identical oracle commit-decision contexts for every model using expected calibration error with utterance-cluster bootstrap intervals. The oracle is derived from the base model’s running-max prefix chain so that models are compared on the same continue-versus-stop decisions. 4 Results 4.1 Single-turn Forced-prefix Decoding Figure 1 compares the three inference mechanisms on the base and single-turn models, and Table 2 summarizes every frontier with attainable-envelope AUC, defined in Appendix A , Equation 6 . Prefix training reduces multi-turn ECE by 63–68% across all evaluated prefixes, and by 68–80% on early prefixes. Relative to the matched multi-turn base, δ = 0.2 \delta=0.2 reduces ECE by 56–63% overall and 65–73% at early prefixes, while δ = 0.5 \delta=0.5 reduces ECE by 27–39% overall and 32–42% at early prefixes. In contrast, single-turn training reduces overall ECE by only 3–11%, while early-prefix ECE worsens by 2–5%. Early-prefix calibration is especially important because low-latency translation requires the model to decide whether to commit from a context containing little audio. The multi-turn results show that dense boundary supervision is associated with improved confidence throughout the utterance, which may help explain the stronger low-latency frontier. Calibration alone does not explain the overall differences among models; the quality of prefix and full-sentence supervision may also contribute. The weak calibration gains of the single-turn model contrast with the text results of Hoang et al. (2026) , despite the analogous training objective. We speculate on some of the reasons why this might be the case and why the multi-turn protocol is the better option for speech translation: • Acoustic segmentation. Text prefixes end at complete word boundaries and are represented by native language-model tokens. Fixed 2 s speech blocks instead contain a variable amount of linguistic content, may end within words or phrases, and are encoded by a frozen audio tower. The decoder must therefore infer both the content and completeness of an acoustically uncertain prefix. • Closing-token semantics. The closing token may retain its pretrained conversational meaning of ending an assistant response rather than acquiring a clean interpretation as “wait for more speech,” weakening the alignment between EOS confidence and translation stability. • Oracle noise. The self-teacher oracle is derived from agreement between complete- and partial-waveform translations. Acoustic ambiguity can make these targets noisier than word-bounded text prefixes even after enforcing monotonicity. • Sequential supervision. Single-turn training samples independent initial-prefix examples, whereas multi-turn training supervises every boundary in order and preserves the preceding sequence of audio blocks, commitments, and explicit empty turns. This context may expose how evidence accumulates and provide a more direct signal for distinguishing continuation from waiting. 5 Conclusion We presented prefix learning for adapting a speech language model to flicker-free simultaneous translation without transcripts or human translations. Training on target prefixes improves the quality–latency frontier for both single-turn forced-prefix and multi-turn decoding. Among the tested inference mechanisms, confidence provides the broadest and most consistently competitive operating range. Under multi-turn training, dense boundary supervision is associated with substantially better confidence calibration across the utterance, including at early prefixes, while single-turn training yields only modest overall gains and no early-prefix improvement. This contrast may help explain why the multi-turn model generally makes better-timed low-latency commitments. A small synthesis margin sometimes extends low-latency coverage, particularly on shorter utterances, whereas a larger margin degrades translation quality and calibration. Prefix adaptation therefore improves simultaneous speech translation, especially under multi-turn append-only decoding, while synthesis density introduces a non-monotonic quality–latency trade-off. 6 Limitations • Experiments cover one base model (Qwen2.5-Omni-7B), three English-source language directions, and read or prompted speech benchmarks. Transfer to other model families, languages, accents, domains, and spontaneous conversational speech remains untested. • Stable-prefix targets are synthesized by the base model using lexical longest-common-prefix agreement with its own full-audio translation. They can inherit self-teacher errors and biases, and lexical stability does not guarantee semantic support or correctness. • Source time advances in fixed 2 2 s blocks with known utterance boundaries. We do not evaluate adaptive segmentation, continuous unsegmented input, network delay, wall-clock decoding latency, throughput, or memory use; Average Lagging measures policy delay only, and the expected computational benefit of key–value cache reuse is not quantified. • Translation quality is measured automatically with COMET, without human evaluation of adequacy, fluency, or the usefulness of partial outputs. Output is monotone by construction, so the system prevents flicker but cannot revise an early erroneous commitment. • Calibration is evaluated on 64 FLEURS oracle chains per direction against base-derived continue-versus-stop labels. The results characterize commit confidence for these oracle commit-decision contexts and prompt representations, not generic language-model calibration, human judgments of semantic certainty, or out-of-domain calibration. • The single-turn and multi-turn comparisons change both the causal representation and the structure of training examples. Without a crossed train–inference representation study, their differences cannot be attributed solely to matching commit-decision contexts. • We did not audit Qwen2.5-Omni’s pretraining data for overlap with the evaluation sets, so benchmark contamination cannot be ruled out.
